steps.en: What you see: An echogenic mass sits in the left ventricular apex, distinct from the surrounding trabeculation. It shows no independent motion of its own and moves only with the wall beneath it. An underlying apical akinesis or aneurysm from an old anterior infarct is almost always present. Contrast study opacifies around the mass when surface views stay poor.

Normal values with units: Normal apical thickness. The apex tapers to a few millimetres and thickens in systole. A mass that never thickens and persists in two planes is not wall.. Source: ASE 2015 chamber quantification guideline, section on left ventricular wall thickness

Thrombus morphology grades. Small flat mural clot confined to the apex. Moderate protruding clot with mobile edges but a broad base. Large pedunculated mobile clot with high embolic risk.. Source: ASE 2019 transthoracic examination guideline, section on apical views

Ejection fraction context. Most thrombi follow large anterior infarcts with ejection fraction below 40 percent and apical akinesis.. Source: ASE 2015 chamber quantification guideline, section on left ventricular ejection fraction

ECG and heart sound correlation ecg: Q waves of a previous anterior infarct mark the territory at risk. Persistent ST elevation suggests an aneurysm beneath the clot. Non specific changes alone never rule out a small mural thrombus.

ECG and heart sound correlation sounds: A third sound marks the dilated infarcted ventricle. A pansystolic murmur marks functional regurgitation when present. No murmur comes from the thrombus itself.

What to report: Mass size in two planes with mobility, attachment base and protrusion
Underlying wall motion defect and aneurysm size with ejection fraction
Gain settings, contrast use and the foreshortening check for audit
Embolic history with the anticoagulation referral plan
Red flags needing urgent referral: Mobile pedunculated clot with an embolic event, needs urgent anticoagulation review
Large protruding clot before cardiac surgery, needs urgent surgical planning review
Stroke with a new apical mass, needs immediate neurology and cardiology review together
Pitfalls: Clots form within days of a large infarct, so image the apex before discharge in every anterior infarct.
Anticoagulation dissolves most clots over months, so schedule interval imaging on referral advice.
A normal study never excludes a small mural clot, so state image quality and rescan when suspicion persists.

todo.en: How to get it on the probe, step by step: Start in the apical four chamber view and slide down until the apex is longest and thinnest.
Lower overall gain and raise near field gain until the blood pool turns dark but the wall stays bright.
Sweep slowly from four chamber to two chamber to long axis to prove the mass in two planes.
Zoom the apex and watch two full cycles for independent motion versus wall tethering.
Use contrast when the apex stays fuzzy, watching it fill around the dark filling defect.
Common mistakes and how to correct them: Calling foreshortened trabeculation a thrombus. Fix: Slide down and laterally until the apex is longest. A cut apex bunches trabeculation into a fake mass.
Scanning with high gain that fills the apex with noise. Fix: Drop gain until the cavity is echo free. High gain fills the apex with noise that mimics clot.
Confusing a vegetation or tumour with a clot. Fix: Vegetations move chaotically on their own while clots ride with the wall. Watch two cycles zoomed.

q.en: How does a clot move compared with a vegetation?

o.en: It rides with the wall and never moves on its own
It shimmers chaotically independent of the wall

why.en: Clots are tethered to dead wall and ride with it, while vegetations shimmer independently on leaflets.

q.en: Trabeculation bunches at the apex mimicking a mass. What first?

o.en: Slide for the longest thinnest apex and lower gain until the pool is dark

why.en: True apical geometry with a dark blood pool separates wall from mass.

q.en: A stroke patient shows a large mobile pedunculated apical mass. What next?

o.en: Urgent anticoagulation review with neurology input

why.en: Mobile clots embolise again without treatment, so urgent anticoagulation review with neurology input follows.

q.en: The apex stays fuzzy after gain work. What confirms the mass?

o.en: Contrast opacification filling around a dark defect

why.en: Contrast fills the cavity around the clot and outlines its true size and mobility.
